input.underspecified_spec: The method is an SSL-augmented few-shot learning approach for image classification. Given a labeled base set for meta-learning and optionally a large generic unlabeled pool, the method proceeds in three phases. (1) If an external pool is used, train a domain classifier (logistic regression on ResNet-101 features) using the base set as positives and pool as negatives, then select a subset of pool images with highest likelihood ratio of belonging to the base domain to serve as the SSL dataset; otherwise, use the base set itself. (2) Jointly train a shared feature backbone (ResNet-18) with a meta-learning objective (prototypical networks) and one or more self-supervised auxiliary tasks (jigsaw puzzle, rotation). Episodes sample N classes, K support, and M query examples from the base labels. The backbone computes embeddings; a supervised loss (cross-entropy over distances between query embeddings and class prototypes) is combined with self-supervised losses (cross-entropy for predicting the permutation index of a jigsaw-transformed image or the rotation angle). When the SSL set differs from the meta-learning set, a separate batch is used for SSL. (3) For novel classes, discard auxiliary losses, compute prototypes from the K support examples using the trained backbone, and classify each query based on its distance to the class prototypes. The method is evaluated on 5-way 5-shot and 20-way 5-shot accuracies on fine-grained datasets (Birds, Cars, Aircrafts, Dogs, Flowers) and mini-ImageNet/tiered-ImageNet against standard meta-learners and prior few-shot methods.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, Fair Robust Learning (FRL), is a training framework for image classification that enforces class-wise fairness in both standard accuracy and adversarial robustness. Given a labeled training set and a separate validation set, it starts from a pre-trained robust model (e.g., from PGD adversarial training) and iteratively reduces performance disparities across classes. The procedure alternates between two phases. (1) Fairness evaluation and adjustment: on the validation set, per-class standard and boundary errors are estimated (boundary error measures the proportion of samples near the decision boundary). For each class, if its error exceeds the average by more than a preset tolerance, Lagrange multipliers for that class are increased proportionally (Reweight) or the class’s adversarial perturbation margin is multiplicatively enlarged (Remargin). (2) Model update: the model is trained for several epochs on the training set with adversarial training using the current class-wise adjustments. Reweight up-weights the standard and boundary loss contributions for violating classes; Remargin generates stronger adversarial examples for those classes by using a larger perturbation radius, improving their robustness. The two strategies can be combined. The loop continues until class-wise error gaps fall within the tolerances. Evaluation reports per-class and average standard, boundary, and robust error rates under a PGD attack, targeting equalized accuracy and robustness across all classes.

input.underspecified_spec: MatchDG is a two-phase approach for domain generalization. In Phase I, a contrastive learning procedure is used: for each anchor image, we select positive samples from the same class but different domains, and negatives from different classes. The model optimizes a temperature-scaled cosine similarity contrastive loss. The matches are updated periodically to the nearest same-class cross-domain neighbors in the representation space. Phase II then computes final matches using the learned representation and trains a classifier to minimize cross-entropy plus an L2 regularizer on matched representations. The technique is tested on domain generalization benchmarks including rotated MNIST/Fashion-MNIST, PACS, and chest X-rays. gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, MatchDG, is a two-phase domain generalization algorithm that learns an object-invariant representation by iteratively refining cross-domain same-class matches. Given labeled images from multiple source domains, Phase I learns a feature map Φ using a contrastive loss where positives are same-class images from different domains and negatives are different-class images, with temperature-scaled cosine similarity. Matches are initially random but are updated every t epochs to the nearest cross-domain, same-class neighbors in the current Φ-space, converging toward true object-level matches. Phase II uses the final Φ to compute fixed nearest-neighbor cross-domain matches and then trains a classifier head h on top of Φ by minimizing the sum of cross-entropy and an ℓ2-distance penalty between matched representations, weighted by λ. The model is evaluated on domain generalization benchmarks: Rotated MNIST/Fashion-MNIST (rotation angles as domains), PACS (photo, art, cartoon, sketch), and Chest X-rays from three sources. Performance is measured by target-domain accuracy, compared against ERM, random-match regularizer, and other domain generalization methods. MatchDG can be extended with data-augmentation-based object matches (MDGHybrid) by adding those pairs as perfect matches in Phase II.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, DirectPred, is a non‑contrastive self‑supervised representation learning approach for images. Given unlabeled images, it proceeds in four phases. (1) For each training batch, generate two augmented views per image. (2) Feed view 1 through an online encoder and a predictor, and view 2 through a target encoder with a stop‑gradient on its output. (3) Periodically, set the predictor weights directly from the statistics of its inputs: maintain a correlation matrix of the online representations, eigen‑decompose it, and construct the predictor as a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues are the square roots of the correlation eigenvalues plus a small fraction ε of the maximum eigenvalue. Optionally, take a few gradient steps on the predictor between these direct settings to refine alignment. (4) Train the online encoder by minimizing the mean squared error between the predictor’s output and the stop‑gradient target representation, with weight decay applied. The target encoder is updated via exponential moving average (or kept identical, depending on the variant). The method is evaluated by training a linear classifier on frozen online representations and reporting top‑1 and top‑5 accuracy on ImageNet, STL‑10, and CIFAR‑10. Baselines include BYOL with gradient‑trained predictors (linear or two‑layer) and SimSiam.

input.underspecified_spec: The multi-level Thompson sampling method for bandits with clustered arms is a sequential decision procedure for stochastic multi-armed bandits where arms are grouped into a known cluster structure (disjoint clusters or a hierarchy) and rewards are Bernoulli or sub-Gaussian. Given a set of arms and the cluster organization, the method proceeds in two selection phases at each time step. (1) Cluster selection: sample a reward estimate for each cluster from its posterior (Beta or Gaussian conjugate form), then pick the cluster with the highest sample. (2) Arm selection: within the chosen cluster, sample per-arm reward estimates from per-arm posteriors and play the arm with the highest sample. For hierarchical clustering, this two-phase logic is applied recursively from the root downward, sampling sub-trees and descending along the argmax path until a leaf arm is reached. After observing reward feedback, the posteriors of the selected arm and all ancestor clusters are updated based on the observed reward. In the contextual variant with linear expected rewards, the per-cluster and per-arm posteriors are Gaussians with mean parameterized as μᵀx and variance proportional to xᵀB⁻¹x, where B and μ are updated via outer product accumulation and regularized least squares. The approach is evaluated on synthetic Bernoulli and linear contextual bandit problems against standard Thompson sampling, UCB-based algorithms, and other cluster-aware baselines using cumulative regret.

input.underspecified_spec: Contrastive Clustering (CC) is an end-to-end online deep clustering method. Given a mini-batch of images, two augmented views per image are generated via random augmentations (ResizedCrop, ColorJitter, Grayscale, HorizontalFlip, GaussianBlur; GaussianBlur omitted for small images). Features are extracted by a shared ResNet-34 backbone trained from scratch. Two heads then operate on the features: an instance-level contrastive head (ICH) maps features to a 128-dimensional subspace and applies NT-Xent loss to pull views of the same instance together and push others apart. A cluster-level contrastive head (CCH) produces soft cluster assignments via a softmax layer, forming an N×M matrix. A contrastive loss (temperature 1.0) is then computed between the two views' cluster assignments to enforce consistency. An entropy regularization term is included to prevent degenerate solutions. The total loss sums the instance and cluster losses and is minimized using Adam (learning rate 0.0003, no weight decay, no scheduler) for 1000 epochs with batch size 256. At inference, the cluster label is the index of the maximum softmax output from CCH. The method is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, ImageNet-10, ImageNet-Dogs, and Tiny-ImageNet using NMI, ACC, and ARI.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, Contrastive Clustering (CC), is an end-to-end online deep clustering method for images. Given a mini-batch of unlabeled images, it proceeds in three phases: (1) For each image, two augmented views are generated using random augmentations (ResizedCrop, ColorJitter, Grayscale, HorizontalFlip, and GaussianBlur; GaussianBlur is omitted for small-sized images) and fed into a shared backbone network (e.g., ResNet) to extract features. (2) Two contrastive heads operate in parallel on these features. The instance-level contrastive head (ICH) maps features to a lower-dimensional subspace and applies a normalized temperature-scaled cross-entropy loss (NT-Xent) to maximize cosine similarity between views of the same instance and minimize similarity between views of different instances. The cluster-level contrastive head (CCH) applies a softmax to produce an N×M matrix of soft cluster assignments (M is the number of clusters). It then computes a column-wise contrastive loss: treating each column of the matrix as a cluster representation, it maximizes cosine similarity between corresponding columns of the two views and minimizes similarity between different columns, plus an entropy term that penalizes unbalanced cluster assignments. (3) The total loss, sum of instance and cluster losses, is minimized end-to-end via Adam. At inference, the cluster assignment for an image is the index with the maximum softmax output from CCH. The method is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, STL-10, ImageNet-10, ImageNet-Dogs, and Tiny-ImageNet using clustering metrics NMI, ACC, and ARI against a diverse set of clustering baselines.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, padding bias mitigation, is a corrective procedure for convolutional neural networks that use SAME padding. Given a CNN architecture and input images, it proceeds in two phases. (1) Enforce even padding: for a network with d downsampling layers, adjust the input height and width to be one more than an integer multiple of two raised to the power d; for example, 225×225 for architectures with five downsampling steps. If images do not meet this constraint, they are resized or padded with the dataset mean. (2) Replace padding mode: in all convolutional layers, substitute zero-padding with a different padding method. The adapted model is then trained or fine-tuned using the original training protocol. The approach is evaluated on tasks such as small object detection by scanning a stimulus across the input to produce a detection score map and computing average precision at multiple IoU thresholds on datasets like BSTLD. Additionally, per-layer filter symmetry and input coverage uniformity are measured, and classification accuracy is assessed on ImageNet. Baselines include the original model with zero-padding and default input size.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, padding bias mitigation, is a corrective procedure for CNNs that use SAME padding to prevent spatial bias artifacts. Given a CNN architecture and an input image size, it proceeds in two phases. (1) Enforce even padding: For a network with d downsampling layers performing SAME padding, constrain the input height H and width W to H = a1*2^d + 1 and W = a2*2^d + 1, where a1, a2 are positive integers (e.g., 225×225 for ResNet models). If images do not satisfy this constraint, resize or pad them with the dataset mean or a suitable fill value. (2) Replace padding mode: In all convolutional layers, substitute 0-padding with symmetric mirror padding that mirrors border pixels and includes the border, ensuring uniform involvement of all input features. The resulting model is trained or fine-tuned using standard protocols. The approach is evaluated on downstream tasks such as small object detection by scanning a stimulus across the input to produce a detection score map and by computing average precision at various IoU thresholds on datasets like BSTLD, measuring blind-spot suppression.

The proxy is implemented as a differentiable optimization layer: for a given input x, CCP iteratively linearizes the convex part of the sigmoid and maximizes the resulting concave proxy minus cost, outputting the modified feature x'. The approach is evaluated on multiple datasets (spam, credit, fraud, financial distress) with various cost functions, compared against a strategy-blind ERM baseline that ignores user responses.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, Key Point Analysis via Contrastive Learning and Extractive Summarization, is a two-component approach for mapping arguments to key points and generating key points from argument collections. Given a topic and arguments with stances, the matching component uses a siamese network trained with contrastive loss: it encodes an argument and a concatenation of topic and key point with a pretrained RoBERTa, mean-pools to sentence embeddings, and computes cosine similarity; the loss is binary cross-entropy that maximizes similarity for matching pairs. The generation component builds a sentence graph from the arguments. Sentences are split, filtered, and assigned quality scores from an external model. Edge weights are pairwise matching scores from the matching model; nodes are connected only when the score exceeds a threshold. A biased PageRank ranks sentences, balancing quality and matching strength, and a diversity constraint selects top-ranked sentences with low overlap to already chosen ones as key points. Finally, arguments are matched to generated key points using the matching model. Evaluation uses mAP for matching and ROUGE/manual rankings for generation on the ArgsKP shared task dataset.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, Learned Reference for Fourier Phase Retrieval, is a learning-aided iterative reconstruction approach. Given a training set of images, it learns a spatial reference signal of the same dimensions, with values between zero and one, that is added to the target before Fourier amplitude measurement. The learning phase operates by unrolling a fixed number of gradient descent steps that solve the phase retrieval problem for each training image: at each step, the phase is estimated as the angle of the current guess, and the amplitude loss is approximated. The reference is optimized by backpropagating the total reconstruction error through the unrolled sequence. In the reconstruction phase, for a new target, a phaseless Fourier magnitude measurement is taken after adding the learned reference, and the target is recovered by initializing an estimate at zero and running the same unrolled gradient descent steps on the amplitude consistency loss. The measurement process uses a Fourier transform and constrains signals to the unit interval; noise is handled by applying non-negative thresholding to measurements. The method is evaluated on image datasets including MNIST, EMNIST, Fashion MNIST, CIFAR10, SVHN, CelebA, and standard test images, measuring PSNR against baselines such as Hybrid Input-Output, Amplitude Flow, Kaczmarz, and flat or random references.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, learned reference for Fourier phase retrieval, is a learning-aided iterative reconstruction approach for recovering an image from phaseless Fourier amplitude measurements when a known additive reference is present. Given training images, it proceeds in two phases: (1) Learning phase: a real-valued reference signal u (same spatial size as images, pixel values in [0,1]) is optimized to minimize total reconstruction error. This is done by unrolling K steps of gradient descent that solve the phase retrieval problem for each training image, with the outer loop updating u by backpropagating through the unrolled network. Each inner step approximates the amplitude loss using the current phase estimate. (2) Reconstruction phase: for a new target x*, measurements y = |F(x* + u)| are captured with the learned u added. Recovery initializes x to zero and runs K forward unrolled gradient descent steps on the same loss, outputting the estimate. The method uses Fourier transform with 4× oversampling as the measurement operator, constrains all pixel values to [0,1], and handles noise by applying ReLU after measurement. Evaluation is performed on several image datasets using PSNR against conventional phase retrieval baselines (HIO, Amplitude flow, Kaczmarz, flat/random references).

input.underspecified_spec: Shifty is a meta-algorithm for fair classification under demographic shift. It takes training data with features, labels, a protected attribute, and a demographic attribute; a fairness definition as a conditional expectation; a confidence level; and a description of possible post-shift demographic marginals as intervals. The method randomly splits the training data into a candidate set and a fairness-test set. A candidate classifier is obtained by minimizing a loss that consists of worst-case reweighted classification error plus a penalty term. The penalty is the worst-case upper confidence bound on post-shift unfairness under the shift distribution. Both terms are evaluated over the set of possible shift distributions using importance weights that are computed from the demographic shift description. On the fairness-test set, a confidence bound on post-deployment unfairness is constructed for the candidate. Fairness measurements for qualifying samples are reweighted with importance weights estimated from that set, and a t-test-based bound is computed. If the bound is within tolerance, the classifier is returned; otherwise, no solution is provided. Evaluated on UCI Adult and UFRGS datasets with demographic parity constraint, compared to Seldonian, Fairlearn, Fairness Constraints, and RFLearn.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, Shifty, is a fair classification meta-algorithm providing high-confidence fairness guarantees under demographic shift. Given a training dataset D of instances (X, Y, S, T) where S is the protected attribute and T is the demographic attribute whose marginal distribution may change, user-specified fairness definitions g, confidence level δ, and a description Q of possible post-shift T marginals as intervals, Shifty returns either a classifier θ or NO SOLUTION FOUND. The method proceeds in three phases. (1) Data partitioning: D is randomly split into a candidate set Dc and a fairness‑test set Df. (2) Candidate selection: A candidate model θc is trained on Dc by minimizing a loss that combines the worst‑case reweighted classification error (over q∈Q) and a penalty equal to the worst‑case estimated post‑shift unfairness. Both terms use importance weights for each demographic value t, computed as the ratio of the post‑shift conditional probability of the fairness event given t to the pre‑shift conditional probability of t given the event, normalized across groups. The conditional probabilities are estimated from Dc. (3) Fairness test: On Df, a high‑confidence upper bound on the post‑deployment unfairness g'(θc) is constructed. First, fairness measurements H_i for samples satisfying the conditioning event are reweighted by the corresponding importance weights (now estimated from Df). A (1‑δ)-confidence bound is obtained via a t‑test: reweighted sample mean plus t‑quantile times the reweighted sample standard deviation over √N. For unknown shift, the supremum of this bound over all q∈Q is taken; for known shift, the exact q is used. If the resulting bound minus the tolerance τ is ≤ 0, Shifty returns θc; otherwise, it returns NSF. The approach is evaluated on the UCI Adult and UFRGS datasets, enforcing constraints such as disparate impact and demographic parity, against baselines Seldonian, Fairlearn, Fairness Constraints, and RFLearn, using metrics of failure rate, accuracy, and NSF probability.

Input: training data with attributes, fairness definition as conditional expectation, confidence level, shift description as intervals. Output: classifier or NSF. Steps: (1) split training data into candidate and fairness-test sets; (2) train candidate on candidate set by minimizing combined loss: reweighted classification error plus penalty equal to worst-case upper confidence bound on post-shift unfairness, both over possible shifts. Reweighting uses importance weights computed from the shift description. (3) On fairness-test set, construct high-confidence upper bound on post-deployment unfairness; fairness measurements for conditioning samples are reweighted with importance weights estimated from that set, and a t-test-based confidence bound is computed. If bound within tolerance, return classifier; else NSF. Evaluated on Adult and UFRGS datasets with demographic parity.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, Shifty, is a fair classification meta-algorithm providing high-confidence fairness guarantees under demographic shift. Given a training dataset D of instances (X, Y, S, T) where S is the protected attribute and T is the demographic attribute whose marginal distribution may change, user-specified fairness definitions g, confidence level δ, and a description Q of possible post-shift T marginals as intervals, Shifty returns either a classifier θ or NO SOLUTION FOUND. The method proceeds in three phases. (1) Data partitioning: D is randomly split into a candidate set Dc and a fairness‑test set Df. (2) Candidate selection: A candidate model θc is trained on Dc by minimizing a loss that combines the worst‑case reweighted classification error (over q∈Q) and a penalty equal to the worst‑case estimated post‑shift unfairness. Both terms use importance weights for each demographic value t, computed as the ratio of the post‑shift conditional probability of the fairness event given t to the pre‑shift conditional probability of t given the event, normalized across groups. The conditional probabilities are estimated from Dc. (3) Fairness test: On Df, a high‑confidence upper bound on the post‑deployment unfairness g'(θc) is constructed. First, fairness measurements H_i for samples satisfying the conditioning event are reweighted by the corresponding importance weights (now estimated from Df). A (1‑δ)-confidence bound is obtained via a t‑test: reweighted sample mean plus t‑quantile times the reweighted sample standard deviation over √N. For unknown shift, the supremum of this bound over all q∈Q is taken; for known shift, the exact q is used. If the resulting bound minus the tolerance τ is ≤ 0, Shifty returns θc; otherwise, it returns NSF. The approach is evaluated on the UCI Adult and UFRGS datasets, enforcing constraints such as disparate impact and demographic parity, against baselines Seldonian, Fairlearn, Fairness Constraints, and RFLearn, using metrics of failure rate, accuracy, and NSF probability.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, Deep Thinking with Recall and Progressive Training, is a recurrent convolutional approach for spatial reasoning tasks (prefix sums, mazes, chess). Given an input problem instance, an embedding convolution projects it to a feature map. The core is a recall‑augmented recurrent block: at each iteration, the current features are concatenated channel‑wise with the original input, passed through a single convolution to restore the channel count, and then processed by a weight‑shared 4‑layer residual block. This block is applied repeatedly; test‑time iterations can be increased beyond training to handle larger problems. A final convolutional head produces a pixel‑wise solution map. Training uses a two‑part loss. In each step, a random partial depth n is chosen, the forward pass runs n iterations to obtain intermediate features; then an additional random k iterations are performed, and the output after n+k iterations is penalized against the ground truth. This progressive loss is combined with the loss from the full m‑iteration pass, weighted by a task‑specific α. The sampling of n and k forces the network to learn iteration‑agnostic incremental improvements. The method is evaluated on prefix sums (train on 32‑bit, test up to 512‑bit), mazes (train 9×9, test up to 201×201), and chess puzzles (train on the easiest 600K, test on harder). Accuracy is measured per output position. Baselines include recurrent networks without recall and feed‑forward ResNets of comparable depth.

input.underspecified_spec: The Exact Feature Distribution Matching (EFDM) method exactly matches the empirical cumulative distribution functions of two equal-size feature vectors. For each channel, both vectors are sorted; the output vector is constructed by assigning each element the value from the sorted target vector at the corresponding rank while preserving the original order of the source vector. The operation is applied channel-wise to deep feature maps. In arbitrary style transfer (AST), a fixed VGG-19 encoder extracts features from content and style images up to relu4_1; EFDM aligns them into a style-transferred feature map, which a randomly initialized decoder maps to the output image. Training minimizes a content loss comparing decoder features to the aligned features, and a style loss that aligns decoder features with style image features at multiple VGG layers (relu1_1, relu2_1, relu3_1, relu4_1). In domain generalization (DG), EFDM is extended as EFDMix by interpolating between the original feature and the style feature using a Beta-distributed mixing weight λ ~ Beta(α,α) with α=0.1. The EFDMix module is inserted into lower-level layers of a pre-trained backbone and activated with probability 0.5 during training; at test time, it is deactivated. Evaluation uses MS-COCO and WikiArt for AST with user preference and visual quality, and PACS classification accuracy and person re-ID mAP for DG.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The Exact Feature Distribution Matching (EFDM) method is a plug‑and‑play feature alignment mechanism for arbitrary style transfer (AST) and domain generalization (DG). Given two equal‑size feature vectors, EFDM exactly matches their empirical cumulative distribution functions by sorting both vectors and assigning each output element the value of the corresponding sorted target while preserving the original order and stopping gradients on the target. The operation is applied channel‑wise to deep feature maps. In AST, a fixed VGG‑19 encoder extracts features from content and style images; EFDM aligns them into a style‑transferred feature map, which a randomly initialized decoder maps to the output image. Training minimizes a content loss (comparing decoder features to the aligned features) and a style loss that aligns decoder features with style image features at multiple VGG layers. In DG, EFDM is extended as EFDMix by interpolating between the original feature and the style feature using a Beta‑distributed mixing weight. The EFDMix module is inserted into lower‑level layers of a pre‑trained backbone and activated with probability 0.5 during training; at test time, it is deactivated. The method is evaluated on AST using MS‑COCO and WikiArt with user preference and visual quality, and on DG using PACS classification accuracy and Market1501/GRID person re‑ID mAP against baselines such as AdaIN, Gatys, CMD, HM, and MixStyle.

input.underspecified_spec: FairCal is a post-training calibration method for face verification. Given a pre-trained face embedding model and a calibration dataset of image pairs with cosine similarity scores and genuine/imposter labels, it first applies K-means clustering (K=100) to the feature embeddings of all images. For each cluster, it collects calibration pairs where at least one image's embedding falls into that cluster, and uses calibration to learn a mapping from similarity scores to conditional match probabilities. For a test pair, cosine similarity is computed and the clusters of the two images are determined. If they are in the same cluster, the output is the probability from that cluster's mapping. If they are in different clusters, the output is a weighted average θ·μ_{k1}(s) + (1−θ)·μ_{k2}(s), where θ is the ratio of the size of the first cluster's calibration set to the sum of sizes of both clusters' calibration sets. Evaluation uses RFW and BFW datasets with 5-fold leave-one-out cross-validation. Metrics include AUROC, TPR at fixed FPRs, subgroup calibration error (KS) and its deviation, and FPR deviations across subgroups. Baselines include cosine similarity thresholding, AGENDA, PASS, FTC, GST, FSN, and an oracle using ground-truth sensitive attributes.

gold.codification_ready_reference: FairCal is a post-training calibration method for fairness in face verification. Given a pre-trained face embedding model and a calibration dataset of image pairs with cosine similarity scores and genuine/imposter labels, the method proceeds in three phases. (1) Unsupervised clustering: Apply K-means to the feature vectors of all images in the calibration set to partition the embedding space into K clusters. (2) Per-cluster calibration: For each cluster k, collect all calibration pairs where at least one image’s embedding falls into cluster k. Use beta calibration to learn a map from cosine similarity scores to calibrated match probabilities conditioned on that cluster, using the labels in the collected set. (3) Pair scoring: For a new pair (x1, x2), compute cosine similarity s and determine cluster memberships. If both images belong to the same cluster k, output the probability μ_k(s). If they belong to different clusters k1 and k2, output a weighted average θ·μ_{k1}(s) + (1−θ)·μ_{k2}(s), where θ is the relative size of cluster k1’s calibration set compared to the sum of the sizes of both clusters’ calibration sets. The method does not require sensitive attributes, retraining, or tuning of the embedding model. Evaluation is performed on the RFW and BFW datasets using leave-one-out cross-validation over five folds. Performance is measured by AUROC, TPR at fixed FPRs, subgroup calibration error (KS) and its deviation, and FPR deviations across subgroups. Baselines include the raw cosine similarity classifier, AGENDA, PASS, FTC, GST, FSN, and an oracle variant that uses ground-truth sensitive attributes in place of unsupervised clusters.

input.underspecified_spec: FOCUS is a gradient-based method for generating counterfactual explanations for tree ensembles. It constructs a differentiable surrogate by replacing hard splits with sigmoid activations along leaf paths, and combining tree outputs via a temperature-scaled softmax. The optimization minimizes a loss that includes a term encouraging the surrogate to reduce the probability of the original class, and a distance term. The loss is minimized via gradient descent starting from the original instance, producing a counterfactual. Hyperparameters such as sigmoid steepness and softmax temperature are tuned jointly over a grid to produce valid counterfactuals for all instances. Evaluation uses four binary classification datasets (Wine, HELOC, COMPAS, Shopping) and comparison against Feature Tweaking and DACE with mean distance, relative distance, and proportion of closer counterfactuals.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method, FOCUS, is a gradient-based optimization approach for generating counterfactual explanations for tree ensemble classifiers. Given an instance x and a trained tree ensemble f, it produces a minimally perturbed counterfactual example x¯. The method proceeds in three phases. (1) Construct a differentiable surrogate f_tilde: For each tree, replace hard split decisions with sigmoid functions centered at the split thresholds (with tunable steepness σ). The probability that a leaf is reached is the product of sigmoids along the path. The tree's output is the weighted sum of leaf distributions by these leaf probabilities. The ensemble output is a softmax (temperature τ) over the weighted sum of individual tree outputs. (2) Define a composite loss: a prediction loss that is active only while the original model f still predicts the same class as for x, given by the surrogate's probability for that class, plus a distance term weighted by β using any differentiable distance function d (e.g., Euclidean, Manhattan, Cosine, Mahalanobis). (3) Minimize this loss via gradient descent starting from x, for a preset number of iterations, yielding the optimal x¯. The explanation is Δ = x¯ - x. The method is evaluated on four binary classification datasets (Wine, HELOC, COMPAS, Shopping) against Feature Tweaking and DACE, using mean distance, mean relative distance, and proportion of closer counterfactuals under multiple distance metrics.

input.underspecified_spec: Label-Free Explainability extends post-hoc feature and example importance techniques to unsupervised models. Given a pre-trained encoder f mapping inputs to a latent space H, and a test input x, the method provides explanations without requiring labels. For feature importance, a scalar auxiliary function g_x is defined to capture the similarity between the representation of x and other inputs in latent space. Any existing linear feature importance method is applied to g_x, yielding per-feature scores which indicate which input features are most influential for the overall representation. For example importance, loss-based methods (e.g., Influence Functions) are adapted by restricting gradient computations to the encoder parameters when applying the unsupervised loss, capturing the impact of removing training examples on the loss for x. Representation-based methods (e.g., KNN in latent space) are directly reused: nearest training representations are retrieved, and importance is assigned via kernel weights or optimization. Evaluation uses consistency checks: perturbing top-scoring features should maximally shift the representation, and top-scoring training examples should share semantic labels with x. The method is demonstrated by comparing representation spaces learned from different self-supervised pretext tasks and by analyzing saliency maps of disentangled VAE units.

input.underspecified_spec: The method sets up a diagnostic VAE to study approximation error on synthetic 2-D Gaussian mixture data. Given samples x ∈ ℝ² from a mixture of four isotropic Gaussians with uniform categorical prior, the VAE uses a factorized Bernoulli encoder and a Gaussian decoder. The encoder first maps x through a two-hidden-layer ReLU network to logits for a 2-bit binary representation of the latent category z∈{1,2,3,4}. The decoder computes Gaussian means via a learnable 2×4 matrix acting on a one-hot encoding of z and uses a shared, fixed isotropic variance. The model is trained by maximizing the ELBO objective via stochastic gradient descent. The evaluation qualitatively compares posterior decision maps of the learned encoder and model posterior against the ground truth and against an RBM trained on the same data. ELBO values are also reported. The setup demonstrates how the ELBO objective distorts the decoder toward a constrained, factorized-posterior-consistent set even when the decoder family contains the true model.

input.underspecified_spec: Label-Free Explainability is a post-hoc wrapper framework for unsupervised and self-supervised representation models. Given a pre-trained latent map f: X→H (e.g., an encoder) and a test input x, the method produces two types of explanations without requiring output labels. For feature importance, an auxiliary scalar function g_x is built that computes the inner product of the fixed representation f(x) with the representation of any input; any linear feature importance method is then applied to g_x, yielding per-feature importance scores that sum to the squared norm of f(x) up to a baseline. For example importance, loss-based methods use the unsupervised training loss L and compute influence scores by differentiating L with respect to the model parameters; representation-based methods directly use latent vectors f(x) and f(x^n), assigning importance via nearest-neighbor kernel weights or via convex optimization that reconstructs f(x) from training representations. The framework is evaluated by measuring latent representation shift when masking top-M important features and by label similarity of top-M training examples. Representations from different pretext tasks are compared via Pearson correlation of saliency maps and example importance vectors. The approach is applied to autoencoders on MNIST and ECG5000, SimCLR on CIFAR-10, and disentangled VAEs on dSprites.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, AMuLaP, is a statistics‑based label mapping technique for few‑shot text classification with prompting. Given a small labeled training set, a manual prompt template, and a pretrained masked language model, it automatically selects multiple label words per class without gradient‑based search. The method proceeds in two stages. In the label selection stage, for each class, the model’s predicted probability distribution over the vocabulary at the [MASK] token is averaged across its training examples, yielding a class‑conditional vector. For each class, the top‑k tokens with highest probabilities from its class‑conditional vector are retained as the label word set. For prediction, the probability for a class is the sum of the masked token probabilities of its selected words, and the class with highest sum is chosen. Optionally, the language model can be fine‑tuned by minimizing cross‑entropy loss using these summed probabilities as class scores. The approach is evaluated on eight GLUE classification tasks (MNLI, MNLI‑mm, SST‑2, QNLI, RTE, MRPC, QQP, CoLA) against baselines including manual prompts, in‑context learning, PETAL, and Auto‑L, reporting accuracy, F1, and Matthews correlation across five random few‑shot splits.

input.underspecified_spec: CrossWalk is a graph reweighting method for fairness-enhanced node representation learning. Given a graph with node group labels, it modifies edge weights to bias random walk based embeddings (e.g., DeepWalk, Node2Vec) so that resulting representations reduce performance disparity across groups in downstream graph tasks. The method proceeds in two phases. (1) For every node v, compute a proximity score m(v) representing its closeness to group boundaries: run a set of truncated random walks of fixed length from v and measure the fraction of steps that land in nodes of different groups. (2) Using m(v) and two tunable parameters α (controls how much weight is shifted to inter-group edges) and p (amplifies boundary bias), update each outgoing edge from v: for a neighbor u in the same group, scale the original edge weight by (1-α)·m(u)^p and normalize across same-group neighbors; for a neighbor in a different group c, scale by α·m(u)^p and normalize per group, dividing by the number of distinct other groups in v's neighborhood. The resulting transition probabilities are used by a random walk embedding method to learn node embeddings. The embeddings are evaluated on the original graph by three tasks: influence maximization via k-medoids seed selection and Independent Cascade diffusion; node classification via Label Propagation; and link prediction via logistic regression on edge features. Performance disparity is measured as the variance of per-group accuracy or infection fraction.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, Deep Learning on a Data Diet, is a data pruning approach for supervised image classification. Given a labeled training set and a network architecture, it proceeds in three phases: (1) Compute per-example importance scores: either the GraNd score as the expected L2 norm of the per-example loss gradient at initialization, or the EL2N score as the expected L2 norm of the error vector (softmax outputs minus one-hot label) early in training, obtained by averaging error norms across multiple short training trajectories. (2) Sort examples by score and select a subset to keep. The basic variant retains a fixed percentage of examples with the highest scores while discarding low-score examples. An improved sliding window variant keeps examples within a score range, discarding both the lowest and very highest scoring examples to account for label noise. (3) Train a new network from scratch on the selected subset using standard training, and evaluate test accuracy. The method is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and CINIC-10 with ResNet architectures, comparing against training on the full dataset and random pruning of the same size.

input.underspecified_spec: The analysis method, single-image self-supervision with aggressive augmentation, is a controlled framework for evaluating self-supervised representation learning under data scarcity. This augmented dataset is combined with any native augmentations of the chosen self-supervised method (BiGAN, RotNet, or DeepCluster) and used to train that method following its original algorithm. After training, the encoder (AlexNet with BatchNorm) is frozen. For each convolutional layer, activations are pooled via adaptive max-pooling, and a linear classifier is trained on the pooled features using the target dataset (ImageNet or CIFAR-10/100). The evaluation metric is top-1 accuracy of these linear probes, computed on the validation set (using 10-crop averaging for ImageNet, full resolution for CIFAR). This framework isolates the effect of source image count on representation quality at different network depths.

Given user history and candidate items, we compute a utility matrix w_ij where each entry reflects the relevance of item j to user i. This is done by embedding items and computing the similarity between the embeddings of the user’s past items and the item. User and item utilities are normalized: user utility is divided by the maximum possible utility for that user, item utility by the total possible utility across all users. We then solve a max-min program: maximize the minimum normalized user utility subject to the constraint that the minimum normalized item utility is at least a fraction γ of its optimal unconstrained value. Third, for a chosen fairness trade‑off parameter γ, a convex max‑min program is solved to obtain a per‑user probability distribution over items. Evaluation measures the achieved minimum normalized user and item utilities, the price of fairness (relative loss in user fairness under full item fairness), and the price of misestimation when only estimated utilities are available. source.original_paper_title: PATE-GAN: Generating Synthetic Data with Differential Privacy Guarantees

input.underspecified_spec: PATE-GAN is a differentially private GAN for generating synthetic data from a supervised dataset. Given a real dataset D and privacy parameters (epsilon, delta), the method partitions D into k disjoint subsets. It proceeds in four phases per generator iteration: (1) Teacher Update: each of k teacher discriminators is updated using real samples from its own partition and fake samples from the generator, trained to classify real vs. fake. (2) Student Labeling: n synthetic samples are generated by G and labeled via PATE_lambda, which aggregates teacher votes with added Laplace noise and outputs the majority label. (3) Student Training: the student discriminator S is updated on these labeled synthetic samples to minimize cross-entropy between its predictions and the noisy teacher labels; the privacy cost of each PATE query is accumulated via a moments accountant with a data-dependent bound. (4) Generator Update: G is updated adversarially against the student to improve the quality of generated samples. Training terminates when the accumulated privacy budget reaches epsilon. The resulting generator G is (epsilon, delta)-differentially private and can produce synthetic feature-label pairs. The approach is evaluated on six tabular datasets (e.g., Kaggle Credit, UCI ISOLET) against DPGAN and a non-private GAN. Utility is measured by training 12 downstream classifiers on synthetic data and testing on real data (AUROC, AUPRC), as well as by Synthetic Ranking Agreement (SRA), which compares the performance ranking of classifiers on synthetic data with their ranking on real data.

input.underspecified_spec: PATE-GAN is a differentially private GAN for generating synthetic data from a supervised dataset. Given a real dataset D and privacy parameters (epsilon, delta), the method partitions D into k subsets. It proceeds in four phases per generator iteration: (1) Teacher Update: each of k teacher discriminators is updated using real samples from its own partition and fake samples from the generator, trained to classify real vs. fake. (2) Student Labeling: n synthetic samples are generated by G and labeled via PATE_lambda, which aggregates teacher votes with added Laplace noise and outputs the majority label. (3) Student Training: the student discriminator S is updated on these labeled synthetic samples to minimize cross-entropy between its predictions and the noisy teacher labels; the privacy cost of each PATE query is accumulated via a moments accountant with a data-dependent bound. (4) Generator Update: G is updated to maximize the student’s confidence in its generated samples, i.e., minimize log(1 - S(G(z))). Training terminates when the accumulated privacy budget reaches epsilon. The resulting generator G is (epsilon, delta)-differentially private and can produce synthetic feature-label pairs. The approach is evaluated on six tabular datasets (e.g., Kaggle Credit, UCI ISOLET) against DPGAN and a non-private GAN. Utility is measured by training 12 downstream classifiers on synthetic data and testing on real data (AUROC, AUPRC), as well as by Synthetic Ranking Agreement (SRA), which compares the performance ranking of classifiers on synthetic data with their ranking on real data.

This sequence is processed by a standard Transformer encoder consisting of L alternating layers of multi-head self-attention (with pre-layer normalization and residual connections) and MLP blocks (two linear layers with GELU activation, pre-norm residual). For fine-tuning on downstream tasks, the pre-training head is replaced by a single linear layer, and training is performed with standard classification loss, optionally at higher resolution where the pre-trained position embeddings are 2D interpolated. The model is evaluated by fine-tuning accuracy on standard image classification benchmarks. The architecture can be scaled across depth, width, and patch size, with larger variants achieving higher performance when pre-trained on massive datasets.

input.underspecified_spec: We analyze competition between factual recall and counterfactual adaptation in autoregressive LMs. Using COUNTERFACT, we construct prompts from triples where the model correctly predicts the factual attribute in isolation. Each prompt follows the format: 'Redefine: s r t_cofa. s r'. We run the model and project residual stream and component outputs (attention heads, MLPs) to vocabulary logits via the unembedding matrix after final-layer normalization. At the last token position, we compute for each head the difference between logits for the counterfactual and factual tokens; positive difference indicates counterfactual support, negative indicates factual support. We identify the heads most strongly supporting the factual mechanism and, in those heads, scale the attention weight from the last token to the attribute position by a tuned scaling factor (grid search over {2,5,10,100}) to enhance factual recall. Mechanism dominance is assessed by comparing final token probabilities.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method is an interpretability analysis pipeline for studying how factual recall and counterfactual adaptation mechanisms compete in autoregressive language models. Given a set of factual triples (subject, relation, attribute) and corresponding counterfactual attributes, it constructs prompts of the form 'Redefine: subject relation counterfactual token. subject relation' that juxtapose the two sources of information. The method then traces the competition by projecting the residual stream at each layer, position, and model component (attention heads and MLP blocks) into vocabulary logits via the unembedding matrix, extracting logit values for the factual and counterfactual tokens. The per-component difference Δ = logit(counterfactual) - logit(factual) indicates the contribution to the counterfactual mechanism. These differences are aggregated across layers and heads to localize the competition and identify heads that promote or suppress each mechanism. Finally, it applies attention modification: in a few heads that strongly support the factual mechanism, the attention weight from the final token position to the attribute position is multiplied by a grid-searched factor α to increase factual recall. The method is evaluated on a 10K-instance filtered COUNTERFACT dataset using GPT-2 small and Pythia-6.9B, assessing mechanism dominance rates, component-level contributions, and attention patterns.

input.underspecified_spec: GOVSIM is a multi-agent simulation platform for evaluating cooperative resource management in LLMs. It defines three common pool resource scenarios (fishery, pasture, pollution) where agents must sustainably harvest a shared regenerating resource. Each simulation run proceeds for T months, with each month consisting of three phases: (1) Strategy: agents review past observations and plan; (2) Harvesting: each agent privately submits a harvest amount; the environment then simultaneously executes all harvests, allocating randomly if total demand exceeds available resource, and publicly reveals each harvest; (3) Discussion: agents engage in open-ended group communication. After harvesting, the remaining resource doubles up to a capacity of 100 units; if the resource falls too low, it collapses permanently. Agents are implemented via a generative architecture that prompts an LLM with scenario rules, historical harvests, and conversation transcripts to produce actions and utterances. A universalization intervention optionally augments the agent memory with the current sustainability threshold to encourage long-term thinking. The evaluation protocol computes metrics over multiple seeds: survival time, survival rate, total gain, efficiency, equality (Gini index), and over-usage ratio. The platform can be used to benchmark various LLMs by running them as agents under identical simulation conditions.

input.underspecified_spec: The method is an interpretability protocol for a frozen GPT-2 small (12 layers, 12 heads). Given templated causal sentences and contrastive perturbed pairs, it analyzes syntactic and semantic processing. (1) Syntactic analysis: for each head in every layer, extract attention weights as the post-softmax pre-V probabilities. Measure P_d as the sum of attention from the delimiter token to all tokens divided by total attention, and P_c as the sum of attention between cause and effect tokens divided by total attention. Aggregate across sentences to produce head heatmaps. (2) Semantic analysis: for each pair, compute losses by passing each layer’s residual stream through the final LayerNorm and unembedding matrix to obtain logits, then cross-entropy. Then, for each head, patch its output (V-weighted sum) from the perturbed run into the original run, applying this to all positions simultaneously, forward-propagate, and measure the absolute difference between the original logit difference and the patched logit difference. Rank heads by this change. Evaluate with attention heatmaps, per-layer loss curves, and patching score matrices on template-generated datasets.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method is an interpretability protocol for a frozen GPT-2 small. It traces causal reasoning by locating model layers and attention heads that process syntactic and semantic cues in causal sentences. The method uses template-generated data and proceeds in three phases. (1) Data generation: fill templates with slot values to create causal sentences with cause–effect relations joined by causal delimiters, and create contrastive pairs by swapping a critical constituent (location/object) to form a nonsensical perturbed sentence. (2) Syntactic analysis: for each sentence, extract per-head attention weights and compute two metrics: the proportion of attention to the causal delimiter and the proportion of attention flowing between cause and effect tokens. Aggregate these metrics across sentences to produce head-level heatmaps. (3) Semantic analysis: for each contrastive pair, compute per-layer token losses by projecting each layer’s residual stream onto the vocabulary; then perform activation patching on attention head outputs by running original and perturbed passes, substituting each head’s activation, and measuring the resulting change in final logit difference. This yields head-level patching scores that indicate sensitivity to semantic perturbations. The pipeline outputs attention fraction heatmaps and patching score matrices across layers and heads, serving as localization maps for syntactic and semantic processing of causal relations.

input.underspecified_spec: The method, FairQCM, is a reinforcement learning algorithm for learning fair policies in non-Markovian fairness settings defined by a multi-stakeholder MDP and a fairness scheme. Given a memory augmentation that makes the stakeholder status function Markovian, and a reward-like fairness scheme where the extended aggregation reduces to a discounted sum of per-step aggregation scores, the algorithm treats the composition W∘U as a reward. Training proceeds in three phases: (1) The agent interacts with the MDP as usual, storing a finite memory that tracks sufficient statistics for the status function. At each step, after executing an action, the real experience includes the current augmented state, action, next augmented state, and reward. (2) Counterfactual experiences are synthetically generated by replacing the current memory with some alternative memory states from the finite set, computing the subsequent memory via the memory update function and the corresponding reward. (3) Both real and counterfactual experiences are used in a Q-learning update (tabular or DQN) to improve the policy. The learned Q-function yields a policy that maximizes expected fairness score. The method is evaluated on resource allocation and simulated lending environments against baselines with various memory mechanisms using accumulated fairness score as metric.

input.underspecified_spec: CroPA (Cross-Prompt Attack) generates adversarial images for vision-language models with high cross-prompt transferability. It supports both targeted and non-targeted settings. Given a clean image, a set of training prompts, and a target text (targeted) or the original clean output (non-targeted), the method proceeds as follows. (1) Initialization: image perturbation is set to zero, and a prompt perturbation is initialized to the embedding of one sampled prompt. (2) Iterative update: For K steps, sample a prompt from the set, add the current prompt perturbation to its embedding, and forward the perturbed image and combined text embedding through the VLM. Compute the language modeling (autoregressive cross-entropy) loss against the target. Update the image perturbation using signed gradient descent (targeted) or ascent (non-targeted), then project the perturbation to the L∞ ε-ball of radius 16/255. (3) Prompt perturbation update: compute the gradient of the same loss with respect to the text embedding and update the prompt perturbation via signed gradient ascent (targeted) or descent (non-targeted) with a separate step size. (4) Evaluation: After optimization, the final adversarial image is used to attack the VLM on a held‑out set of prompts. Performance is measured by Attack Success Rate (ASR): targeted ASR counts exact matches to the target text, non‑targeted ASR counts any output differing from the clean prediction.

input.underspecified_spec: The framework, a multimodal debate protocol for visual question answering, uses two sighted vision-language expert models and a blind text-only judge. It operates on a set of expert models and a dataset of (image, question) pairs. In Phase 1 (disagreement sampling), all expert pairs are evaluated on the dataset, and only samples where two experts predict different answers are retained. In Phase 2 (debate generation), for each disagreement, the two experts receive the image, question, and their preferred answer. Over two rounds, they produce an image description and state premises supporting their answer (Round 1), then rebut the opponent’s arguments using image observations (Round 2), forming a transcript. In Phase 3 (blind judging), a text-only judge sees the transcript and the two image descriptions. It evaluates each premise using several quality criteria, filters high-scoring premises, and selects the better-supported answer. In Phase 4, a separate reasoning extractor takes the judge’s verdict and descriptions to produce a detailed, image-grounded reasoning trace as if it could see the image. In Phase 5, vision-language models are fine-tuned with LoRA to generate such traces from (image, question) pairs, using debate-derived traces as training data. Evaluation is out-of-domain: traces from two datasets are used for fine‑tuning, and the model is tested on a held‑out third dataset. A consultancy baseline replaces debate with a single-expert dialogue, where the same blind judge asks probing questions over two rounds and adjudicates; the same judgement and trace extraction steps apply.

input.underspecified_spec: We study the learning dynamics of RNNs trained in closed-loop control tasks. The RNN has 100 tanh units and is trained on a double integrator with partial position observation, where initial states are uniform in [-2,2]^2. Training uses backpropagation through the environment over 50-step episodes, minimizing cumulative squared state error with SGD (lr 0.01, batch 100, gradient clip 1.0). During training, effective linear feedback gains are estimated from rollouts. The eigenvalues of the coupled agent-environment system are monitored to detect stability changes. A reduced effective model is used to analyze stage-wise behavior. Three learning stages emerge: an initial phase of unstable oscillations, a plateau where eigenvalues compete in a zig-zag pattern, and a final refinement stage with stable damping. The analysis is complemented by comparing open-loop supervised training, where a student RNN imitates a teacher or LQR controller on Gaussian noise inputs.

gold.codification_ready_reference: The method analyzes closed-loop RNN training on a double integrator control task. The environment is linear with state [position, velocity] and observation only position; the cost is cumulative squared distance to origin. An RNN with tanh activation and parameters W, m, z is trained by unrolling through the environment and backpropagating the total cost to update weights via SGD with gradient clipping (policy gradients). An open-loop baseline trains a student RNN via supervised MSE on i.i.d. noise inputs to imitate a teacher pre-trained on the same task or an LQR controller. Learning is examined in three stages via the coupled system matrix P = [A, B z^T; m C A, W]. Stage 1: loss drops, output aligns to negative position, eigenvalue pair of P becomes complex-conjugate unstable. Stage 2: loss plateaus, eigenvalues zig-zag toward stability as the RNN begins representing velocity; this is captured by a surrogate loss balancing short-term control and long-term stability. Stage 3: refinement with stabilized eigenvalues and emergence of a second slow real mode. Diagnostics include extracting effective linear feedback gains from trajectories, spectral tracking of P, and a reduced rank-1 model with scalar overlaps σ. The analysis extends to a multi-frequency tracking task where stage-like frequency acquisition occurs. Evaluation uses test loss on held-out initial states and per-frequency accuracy.

input.underspecified_spec: UADF (Uncertainty-Aware Dynamic Fusion) is a training-free late fusion method for generative error correction (GER) in automatic speech recognition. Given an N-best hypotheses list from an ASR system and the raw speech utterance, the method fuses token-level logits from a GER LLM and an independent ASR model during auto-regressive decoding. It proceeds in three phases. (1) Calibration: Both models' logits are temperature-scaled using parameters τ₁ (LLM) and τ₂ (ASR) found by binary search on a small validation set, matching average confidence to 1 - token error rate. (2) Token-level combination: At each decoding step, the LLM's uncertainty is computed as the entropy of its calibrated predictive distribution. The ASR logits are weighted by σ(uncertainty), and the final logit is the softmax of the sum: calibrated LLM logits plus weighted calibrated ASR logits. (3) Decoding: The next token is selected greedily from this combined distribution, and the process repeats. The ASR model used is Whisper-tiny with its decoder aligned to the LLM's tokenizer and embedding space; the LLM is a LLaMA-7B fine-tuned via LoRA for H2T mapping. UADF is evaluated on the WSJ, ATIS, and CHiME-4 clean/noisy ASR datasets, and on LRS3 for audio-visual ASR, against early fusion, mid fusion, static late fusion, and GER baselines, using word error rate (WER) and word error rate reduction (WERR).
